text.title: Market Analysis Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules constraining a market-analysis artefact: how the market boundary is defined, how segments must partition it, how growth rates and regulatory instruments are recorded, and the decision hook every PEST/STEEP force must carry.

rule.statement: `market_definition` MUST be written as a pass/fail test over (buyer type, need served, substitutability, geography, channel) and applied on record to at least 3 named borderline companies with an in/out verdict each. A category noun alone ("the CRM market") is rejected.

rationale.source: US DOJ/FTC Horizontal Merger Guidelines — hypothetical monopolist (SSNIP) test

rule.rationale: A boundary you cannot apply to a specific company silently widens between sections: the growth rate is taken from a broad definition and the competitor set from a narrow one, so the report describes two different markets and nobody notices because both halves cite sources.

rule.statement: `segments` MUST partition the defined market with no overlap; segment sizes MUST sum to the stated total within ±10%, and any residual MUST appear as an explicit named "other" row rather than being absorbed silently.
rule.rationale: Overlapping segments double-count the same revenue, so the sum exceeds the market and every share calculation downstream is deflated; an unnamed residual is where the segment you actually sell into hides.

rule.statement: Segments MUST be cut by buyer-side attributes — job to be done, purchase trigger, budget owner, buying-committee shape — not by vendor product category. A segment named after a product line ("BI tools", "point solutions") is rejected.
rule.rationale: Product-category segments mirror the incumbent's org chart, so a substitute arriving from a different category is structurally invisible to the analysis — and that substitute is the single event most likely to invalidate the market read.

rule.statement: Every growth figure MUST record base year, terminal year, the underlying unit (revenue / units / seats / installed base), and the publisher. Two CAGRs from different publishers MUST NOT be chained or averaged.
rule.rationale: A seat CAGR equals a revenue CAGR only if price per seat is flat, which it is not under land-and-expand or per-seat discounting; and chaining CAGRs compounds the publishers' differing market definitions, so the terminal number inherits an error nobody can decompose.

rule.statement: Each `regulation_notes` entry MUST name the instrument (regulation/directive/statute number), the jurisdiction, and BOTH the entry-into-force date and the date-of-application for the obligation being cited, distinguishing the two.
rule.rationale: Entry into force and applicability diverge by years: treating "in force" as "applies now" pulls a compliance-driven demand spike forward by that gap, and the roadmap gets built for a buying window that has not opened.

rule.statement: Every PEST/STEEP entry in `forces` MUST name the specific decision it would change (pricing, roadmap item, channel, hiring), the direction of the change, and the observable that would signal the force is moving. Forces with no attached decision are cut, not kept "for context".
rule.rationale: A force with no decision hook is never revisited, so it is never falsified; the PEST table degrades into a list of true statements that survives every review because nothing in it can fail.

rule.statement: Do NOT run when (a) the "market" is a single named account or a captive internal customer — there is no seller set to analyse; (b) the question is only "how big" — route to market-research-tam-sam-som; (c) the product has no identifiable substitute or incumbent budget line yet — route to jtbd-switch-interview and continuous-discovery first; (d) the decision executes inside the current quarter, where a 12-24 month forces read cannot change it.
rule.rationale: Each of these produces a report whose segments and forces sections are structurally empty, and an empty section filled with plausible prose is the failure mode this methodology is meant to prevent.
